title: We spent a year building the step that grades AI strategies, not the one that writes them. Here is what broke.
author: Vegetable-Rub-8241
selftext:
Someone posted a year-long field report here last week ending on "AI accelerates the process, you own the edge through validation". I agree with all of it. This post is about the second half of that sentence, because owning the validation is easy to say and about a third of what we built to do it did not survive contact.



Context so you can weight this: my co-founder wrote his Master's thesis in Mathematics and Finance at Imperial on exactly this problem, a multi-agent pipeline where an LLM proposes factors and a deterministic harness scores them. The rule from the first day was that the model never influences its own reward. I have been building the product around it since.



**THE PROBLEM EVERYONE EVENTUALLY HITS**



A holdout stops being a holdout the moment you use it to choose. Grade fifty candidates against the same unseen window and ship the survivor, and you have fit to that window through selection rather than training. The model never saw it. You did, and you picked with it. Throughput makes this worse, not better, which is why an automated pipeline is the most dangerous version of this setup and not the safest.



**WHAT WE BUILT AGAINST IT**



Deflated Sharpe and deflated IC, discounted by the number of trials. This works, but only if your trial count is truthful, and it has to include everything you killed. Almost nobody logs the discards. \[SLOT: euer echter Trial-Count\]



CSCV probability of backtest overfitting. Better than deflation alone, because it does not depend on you counting your own attempts truthfully.



Progressive reveal, which is the one I would actually recommend to people here. Instead of one holdout you reveal the dev data block by block, so every generation is partly scored on data no earlier selection round could have touched. It prevents the selection ratchet instead of detecting it afterwards. It also makes every result look worse, which is roughly how you know it is working.



**WHAT FAILED**



Our selection objective had five axes. One of them was robustness. We deleted it, because the search learned to game the robustness metric instead of becoming robust. That is the entire problem in miniature: any metric inside the optimisation loop eventually becomes a target. The only defences that held were the ones the proposing model could not see or influence.



We also run a non-LLM genetic programming baseline through the identical controller and the identical scoring seam, so the only thing that differs is the proposal step. If you want to know whether the LLM is adding anything or just adding cost, that is the only way I know to answer it with something other than vibes. \[SLOT: was kam raus? Wenn ihr es noch nicht sauber gemessen habt, schreib genau das\]



**WHAT I WANT FROM THIS POST**



Not signups, there is nothing to sign up for yet. Two questions:



If you run automated search, do you keep a trial counter that persists across sessions, or is it a discipline thing? Everyone I have asked says the second.



What is your defence against the selection ratchet, if you have one that is not "look at it less"?



Blunt answers and "you are solving a problem nobody has" answers both equally welcome.
